title: The Mineral Revolution: Diamonds
summary: The discovery of diamonds near Kimberley, the dispute over Griqualand West, the growth of Kimberley, Cecil Rhodes and De Beers, the compound system and the effects on southern Africa.

notes.text: In **1867** a child found a shiny stone on a farm near Hopetown on the Orange River; it was a 21-carat diamond, later called the **Eureka**. In 1869 the much larger **Star of South Africa** was found. In **1871** rich diamond deposits were found on the farm of the De Beer brothers, where the town of **Kimberley** grew up around the 'Big Hole'.

The area was claimed by the **Griqua** under Nicolaas Waterboer, the **Orange Free State**, the **South African Republic (Transvaal)** and the **Batlhaping** (Tswana). In 1871 a British-appointed judge, Lieutenant-Governor **Keate**, awarded the land to Waterboer, who then asked for British protection. Britain annexed the area as **Griqualand West**, gaining control of the world's richest diamond fields. The Free State was later paid £90 000 in compensation.

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: The **Mineral Revolution** is the name for the huge economic and social changes that followed the discovery of diamonds (1867) and gold (1886). South Africa changed from a farming economy to an industrial, mining economy.

items: At first thousands of individual **diggers** of all races worked small claims with picks and shovels.
As the pits went deeper, claims collapsed and flooded; expensive steam pumps and machinery were needed.
Small diggers sold out to companies that could afford the machinery.

**Cecil John Rhodes** bought up claims and formed **De Beers Consolidated Mines** in **1888**, after buying out his rival Barney Barnato. De Beers controlled almost all diamond production in the world.

notes.text: Mining needed thousands of workers. Black men came from across southern Africa, including Basotho, Bapedi, Tsonga and others, often to earn money to buy **guns**, cattle or to pay taxes. From the 1880s, black workers were forced to live in closed **compounds**: fenced, guarded barracks near the mines.

rows: To stop diamond theft (illicit diamond buying)
Workers could not leave the compound for the length of their contract, often months
To control workers and prevent strikes
Workers were strip-searched; they could buy food only at company stores
Men lived away from their families; wages stayed low

notes.text: White workers were not placed in compounds and were given skilled, better-paid jobs. This **racial division of labour** became the pattern for later mining and industry in South Africa.

items: Kimberley grew into the second-largest town in southern Africa, with the first electric street lights in the southern hemisphere (1882).
Railways were built from the coast to Kimberley.
Britain became more interested in controlling the interior, leading to wars against African kingdoms and the Boer republics.
Migrant labour and the compound system weakened African farming societies.
Mining profits made people like Rhodes very rich and powerful.
